passage.en: Several Enlightenment thinkers questioned the belief that a king's power came from God and could never be challenged. John Locke argued against this, insisting that a ruler held power only with the consent of the people governed. Building on this, Jean-Jacques Rousseau described government as resting on an agreement between citizens and those who represented them. Baron de Montesquieu went further still, arguing that government power should never sit in one pair of hands - he proposed splitting it into three separate branches: one to make laws, one to enforce them, and one to judge disputes under them. This three-way split was first put into practice in the United States, once its thirteen colonies broke away from British rule. The success of the American system, and the rights it guaranteed its citizens, later shaped how political thinkers in France imagined their own government.
